Reproducing Davatolhagh et al. (2025) from dandiset 001712¶

Paper. Davatolhagh MF, Couto J, Melin M, Oesch LT, Findling C, Morales P, Hong I, International Brain Laboratory, Churchland AK (2025). Altered use of prior expectations and modified neural dynamics in a mouse model of autism. bioRxiv, version 1. doi:10.1101/2025.09.12.675910. This attempt used the full text of the preprint (CC-BY-NC-ND).

Dandiset. DANDI:001712, version draft. The paper cites no version, and the dandiset has no published version: the archive lists only the draft. The draft is used, with its modification time (2026-05-28T10:04:28Z) and the ids and sizes of the three assets read, which the next cell checks against the archive. A draft can change; if the check reports a difference, the numbers below may not match the attempt record.

What the dandiset holds. One session (2023-11-14) of one mouse, FD-28, in the biased choice-world task with widefield imaging: a processed NWB file, a raw NWB file and three camera videos. The paper analyses 11 wild-type and 8 Nrxn1a knockout mice with 10 sessions each. The genotype of FD-28 is not stated in the files or the dandiset's metadata, nor in the public IBL database (queried by hand during the attempt, not in this notebook). The findings that compare genotypes cannot be tested; those that the paper states for mice of both genotypes are tested on this session.

Code read. The paper links churchlandlab/chiCa for its encoding analyses (read at commit d98b3c6) and jcouto/wfield for preprocessing (commit 0befe16). The dandiset links the conversion code catalystneuro/IBL-widefield-to-nwb (commit 4a6fb06). Choices that follow them are given in the helper module wfprior.py.

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import optimize, stats

import wfprior as wf

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
info = wf.draft_info()
print(f"dandiset {wf.DANDISET_ID} version {wf.DANDISET_VERSION}, modified {info['modified']}")
for path, (aid, size) in sorted(info["assets"].items()):
    print(f"  {size / 1e9:7.2f} GB  {aid}  {path}")
diff = wf.check_assets(info)
print("Assets differ from those this entry was written against:" if diff else
      "The assets read match those this entry was written against.", *diff, sep="\n")

f = wf.open_nwb(wf.PROCESSED)
trials = wf.load_trials(f)
svd = wf.load_svd(f)
frame_t = svd["t"]
movement = wf.load_movement(f, frame_t)
print(f"loaded trials, imaging components and movement in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

One subject and one session. The subject record has no genotype, and its description is the paper's general description of the cross (KO and wild-type littermates). The paper (Methods) and the file's keywords give the indicator as GCaMP6s, while both imaging planes say GCaMP6f. The dandiset's own keywords and description name "CNTNALP2" (printed above), a different gene from the Nrxn1a of the paper and the file.

The contrasts are in percent (0 to 100) and the five values of the description occur with similar counts. The first block is the 90 unbiased trials the description gives, and the stimulus side follows the block probabilities (about 0.8 on the likely side). A counter-clockwise turn is the correct response to a right stimulus on every trial with a visible stimulus, which confirms the coding of rightward choices. The go cue and the photodiode-detected stimulus onset are close to simultaneous, as the description says (offsets printed above). The wheel movement onset is described as the first movement after the go cue, but some onsets fall before the go cue and the stimulus onset (counts above); those trials are left out of reaction-time measures.

Lab metadata groups in the processed file: ['devices', 'experiment_description', 'experimenter', 'ibl_metadata', 'institution', 'keywords', 'lab', 'optophysiology', 'protocol', 'related_publications', 'session_id', 'source_script', 'subject']

The Methods give 30 frames per second per channel; the timestamps give 31.2 Hz, with regular intervals, and the raw file's imaging plane states 15 Hz. The raw and the processed file hold the same recording (same timestamps), so it is counted once. The spatial components are orthonormal, so variance in pixel space is the sum of the variances of the temporal components. They cover every pixel of the frame: there is no brain mask. The conversion code's documentation says the processed file holds landmarks and a registration to the Allen atlas (lab_meta_data localization, atlas_registration); neither file holds them, so no pixel can be assigned to a cortical area. The reconstructed values are of the order of a few percent, consistent with dF/F.

# Where the ROI of each motion energy series lies, against the median position of the nose tip and the pupil
# centre (mean of the four pupil points) in the same camera, from frames with likelihood 0.9 or more.
import re
def median_xy(cam, part):
    g = f[f"processing/pose_estimation/{cam}Camera/PoseEstimationSeries{part}"]
    xy = g["data"][:]
    return np.nanmedian(xy[g["confidence"][:] >= 0.9], axis=0)
for cam in ("Left", "Right", "Body"):
    desc = f[f"processing/motion_energy/{cam}CameraMotionEnergy"].attrs["description"]
    w_, h_, x0, y0 = map(int, re.search(r"(\d+) pixels wide, (\d+) pixels tall, top-left corner at \((\d+), (\d+)\)", desc).groups())
    print(f"{cam} camera ROI: x {x0} to {x0 + w_}, y {y0} to {y0 + h_}")
    if cam == "Body":
        print("  tail start", median_xy(cam, "TailStart").round())
        continue
    nose = median_xy(cam, "NoseTip")
    pupil = np.mean([median_xy(cam, f"RightPupil{s}") for s in ("Top", "Bottom", "Left", "Right")], axis=0)
    print(f"  nose tip {nose.round()}, pupil centre {pupil.round()}; ROI centre ({x0 + w_ / 2:.0f}, {y0 + h_ / 2:.0f}); "
          f"ROI centre between the two in x: {min(nose[0], pupil[0]) < x0 + w_ / 2 < max(nose[0], pupil[0])}, "
          f"below the pupil: {y0 + h_ / 2 > pupil[1]}")

The camera rates match the Methods (left 60 Hz, right 150 Hz, body 30 Hz). The ROI motion energy descriptions give the ROI's position in pixels but not the body part. In each side camera the ROI centre lies between the nose tip and the pupil and below the pupil (printed above), where the whisker pad is. The body camera's ROI contains the median position of the tail start, so it covers the body. These are taken to be the whisker pads and the body, as the paper's model uses; the positions agree with that, but the files do not name the body parts.

# Clock checks. (1) The wheel turns the way the choice says, after the movement onset of the trial table.
wt = movement.wheel_velocity.to_numpy()
on = wf.frame_index(frame_t, trials.wheel_movement_onset_time.fillna(trials.choice_registration_time).to_numpy())
lags = np.arange(-15, 16)
vel = np.stack([wt[on + k] for k in lags])
sign = np.where(trials.choice_right == 1, 1, -1)
signed = (vel * sign[None, :])[:, ok.to_numpy()]
print("Wheel velocity (rad/s) times choice sign (+1 right), median over trials, by frame from movement onset:")
print(pd.Series(np.median(signed, axis=1), index=lags).round(3).to_string())
print("Wheel position reference frame:", wf.text(f, "processing/wheel/WheelPosition/reference_frame"))
after = vel[15 + 3:15 + 10][:, ok.to_numpy()].mean(0)
ccw = (trials.mouse_wheel_choice == "counter_clockwise").to_numpy()[ok.to_numpy()]
print(f"Mean wheel velocity 0.1 to 0.3 s after movement onset: negative on {(after[ccw] < 0).mean():.3f} of counter-clockwise choices, "
      f"positive on {(after[~ccw] > 0).mean():.3f} of clockwise choices")

# (2) Licks follow rewarded feedback.
licks = f["processing/lick_times/EventsLickTimes/timestamps"][:]
def lick_rate(t0, a, b):
    return np.array([((licks >= t + a) & (licks < t + b)).sum() / (b - a) for t in t0])
fb = trials.feedback_time.to_numpy()
rew = trials.is_mouse_rewarded.to_numpy()
for name, (a, b) in {"-1 to 0 s": (-1, 0), "0 to 1 s": (0, 1)}.items():
    print(f"Lick rate {name} from feedback: rewarded {lick_rate(fb[rew], a, b).mean():.2f}/s, "
          f"unrewarded {lick_rate(fb[~rew], a, b).mean():.2f}/s")

# (3) Imaging and the trial table. Two contrasts, each as the norm in pixel space of the difference between the mean
# responses of two trial groups, by frame from the event, baseline -0.6 to -0.3 s before it. Null: the labels permuted
# within strata (200 permutations), which keeps any difference that comes from the strata.
#   feedback: rewarded against unrewarded trials, strata = absolute contrast;
#   stimulus: right against left stimulus at 25 and 100% contrast, strata = block type.
strong = (trials.gabor_stimulus_contrast >= 25).to_numpy()
right = (trials.gabor_stimulus_side == "right").to_numpy()
onset = wf.frame_index(frame_t, trials.gabor_stimulus_onset_time.to_numpy())
feedback = wf.frame_index(frame_t, trials.feedback_time.to_numpy())
fps = 1 / np.median(np.diff(frame_t))
clk_lags = np.arange(-19, 17)

def clock_check(event_frames, label, strata, rng):
    seg = np.stack([svt[o + clk_lags] - svt[o - 19:o - 9].mean(0) for o in event_frames])
    def course(lab):
        return np.linalg.norm(seg[lab].mean(0) - seg[~lab].mean(0), axis=1)
    null = []
    for _ in range(200):
        perm = label.copy()
        for s_ in np.unique(strata):
            m = strata == s_
            perm[m] = rng.permutation(label[m])
        null.append(course(perm))
    out = pd.DataFrame({"s": np.round(clk_lags / fps, 3), "true": course(label), "null_95th": np.percentile(null, 95, axis=0)}).set_index("s")
    above = out.true > out.null_95th
    run = above & above.shift(-1, fill_value=False) & above.shift(-2, fill_value=False)
    first = out.index[(out.index > -0.3) & run.to_numpy()]
    return out, int(above[out.index < 0].sum()), (first[0] if len(first) else None)

rng_clk = np.random.default_rng(7)
fb_course, fb_pre, fb_first = clock_check(feedback, trials.is_mouse_rewarded.to_numpy(), trials.gabor_stimulus_contrast.to_numpy(), rng_clk)
st_course, st_pre, st_first = clock_check(onset[strong], right[strong], trials.block_type.to_numpy()[strong], rng_clk)
both = pd.concat({"feedback: rewarded vs not": fb_course, "stimulus: right vs left": st_course}, axis=1)
print(f"Feedback: {int(trials.is_mouse_rewarded.sum())} rewarded, {int((~trials.is_mouse_rewarded).sum())} unrewarded trials; "
      f"stimulus: {int((strong & right).sum())} right, {int((strong & ~right).sum())} left trials")
print(both.round(3).to_string())
for name, pre, first in (("feedback", fb_pre, fb_first), ("stimulus", st_pre, st_first)):
    print(f"{name}: frames before the event above the null 95th percentile {pre} of {int((clk_lags < 0).sum())}; "
          f"first of three consecutive frames above it at {first} s")
lick_lat = [licks[(licks > t) & (licks < t + 1)].min() - t for t in fb[rew] if ((licks > t) & (licks < t + 1)).any()]
print(f"First lick after rewarded feedback (video clock): median {np.median(lick_lat):.3f} s over {len(lick_lat)} trials")
rts = trials.rt[strong & ok.to_numpy() & (trials.rt > 0).to_numpy()]
print(f"Movement onset after the stimulus on the stimulus-contrast trials: median {rts.median():.3f} s")

The wheel starts to turn at the trial table's movement onset, and licking rises after rewarded feedback and not after unrewarded feedback, so the wheel, the lick times and the trial table share a clock. The direction disagrees with the descriptions: the wheel series say counter-clockwise is positive, but trials labelled counter_clockwise turn the wheel with negative velocity. The choice labels agree with the rewards (above), so one of the two sign conventions is misdescribed; the analysis uses the choice labels.

For both contrasts the difference stays below the null's 95th percentile on every frame before the event (0 of 19). After feedback the rewarded-unrewarded difference exceeds the null from 0.224 s, close to the median first lick after a reward on the video clock (0.216 s), as expected if licking drives the cortical signal and the imaging, the cameras and the trial table share a clock. After the stimulus the right-left difference exceeds the null only from 0.256 s, later than a visual latency; on these trials the median movement onset is 0.086 s, so the side difference may come from the choice movement. The checks are consistent with a shared clock to within a few frames; they do not show a visual response at its expected latency.

Result: not reproduced. Over 750 trials the Spearman correlation between absolute contrast and reaction time is -0.053 (p = 0.15), so the test of the criterion fails; the median at 0% (0.089 s) does exceed that at 100% (0.081 s). Reaction times are short at every contrast (medians 0.081 to 0.095 s). Of the 899 choice trials with a movement onset, 149 have it at or before the stimulus onset and 346 within 0.08 s after it, so many onsets in the trial table may mark movements begun before the stimulus could guide them. The result depends on this. With reaction times above 0.15 s only (226 trials) the correlation is -0.226 (p = 0.00062). The response time, from stimulus onset to choice registration, is shorter at higher contrast over all 911 choice trials (rho -0.134, p = 5.2e-05; medians 0.326 s at 0% and 0.281 s at 100%). These variants do not change the outcome, as the criterion and the paper's "time to first movement" use the movement onset. The paper's text does not say how the first movement is detected or how movements before the stimulus are treated.

Result: reproduced. At 0% contrast the mouse chose right on 0.831 of trials (74 of 89) in right-likely blocks and 0.507 (37 of 73) in left-likely blocks, a difference of 0.325 (one-sided Fisher p = 9.2e-06). The difference is 0.182 to 0.458 at every signed contrast except +100%, where both blocks give 1.000, and the psychometric bias moves by 19.41% contrast between left-likely (2.86) and right-likely (-16.54) blocks. Whether the shift is smaller than in wild-type mice cannot be tested on one mouse of unknown genotype.

fig2ef-block-adaptation¶

After a block switch, mice adapt their choices toward the newly likely side, and the proportion of choices toward the block side rises from an initial value A to an asymptote B with a time constant tau.

In [14]:
def switch_curve(sel):
    rows = []
    for bi in sorted(trials.block_index.unique()):
        if bi < 2:   # switches between biased blocks: from block 1 to 2 onward
            continue
        g = trials[(trials.block_index == bi)]
        toward_right = g.block_type.iloc[0] == "right_block"
        for k, (i, t) in enumerate(g.iterrows()):
            if k >= 40:
                break
            if not np.isfinite(t.choice_right) or not sel(t):
                continue
            rows.append({"block": bi, "t": k, "toward": float(t.choice_right == (1.0 if toward_right else 0.0))})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def model(t, A, B, tau):
    return B - (B - A) * np.exp(-t / tau)

def adaptation(df, label):
    curve = df.groupby("t").toward.mean()
    (A, B, tau), cov = optimize.curve_fit(model, curve.index.to_numpy(float), curve.to_numpy(), p0=[0.5, 0.8, 5],
                                          bounds=([0, 0, 0.01], [1, 1, 200]))
    early = df[df.t <= 4].toward; late = df[(df.t >= 20) & (df.t <= 39)].toward
    _, p = stats.fisher_exact([[late.sum(), len(late) - late.sum()], [early.sum(), len(early) - early.sum()]], alternative="greater")
    print(f"{label}: {df.block.nunique()} switches, {len(df)} trials; fit A = {A:.3f}, B = {B:.3f}, tau = {tau:.2f} trials "
          f"(SE {np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))[2]:.2f}); toward block side trials 0-4 {early.mean():.3f} (n = {len(early)}), "
          f"trials 20-39 {late.mean():.3f} (n = {len(late)}), one-sided Fisher p = {p:.2g}")
    return curve, (A, B, tau)

sw_all = switch_curve(lambda t: True)
print("Block lengths of the switches used:", trials[trials.block_index >= 2].groupby("block_index").size().tolist())
curve_all, par_all = adaptation(sw_all, "All contrasts")
curve_low, par_low = adaptation(switch_curve(lambda t: t.gabor_stimulus_contrast <= 12.5), "Variant, contrast 12.5% or less")

# Bootstrap over switches: switches drawn with replacement and the curve refitted (500 draws).
rng_sw = np.random.default_rng(202)
blocks_ = sw_all.block.unique()
boot_par = []
for _ in range(500):
    d = pd.concat([sw_all[sw_all.block == b] for b in rng_sw.choice(blocks_, len(blocks_))])
    c = d.groupby("t").toward.mean()
    try:
        boot_par.append(optimize.curve_fit(model, c.index.to_numpy(float), c.to_numpy(), p0=[0.5, 0.8, 5], bounds=([0, 0, 0.01], [1, 1, 200]))[0])
    except RuntimeError:
        boot_par.append([np.nan] * 3)
boot_par = pd.DataFrame(boot_par, columns=["A", "B", "tau"])
print(f"Bootstrap over switches: {int(boot_par.tau.isna().sum())} of {len(boot_par)} fits failed")
print(boot_par.quantile([0.025, 0.5, 0.975]).round(3).to_string())
print(f"Fraction of draws with B > A: {(boot_par.B > boot_par.A).mean():.3f}; with B at its bound (0.999 or more): {(boot_par.B >= 0.999).mean():.3f}; "
      f"with tau of 40 trials or more: {(boot_par.tau >= 40).mean():.3f}")

# Variant: maximum-likelihood fit on the single trials (Bernoulli), which weights each trial number by its count.
t_, y_ = sw_all.t.to_numpy(float), sw_all.toward.to_numpy()
def nll_ad(p):
    q = np.clip(model(t_, *p), 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    return -np.sum(y_ * np.log(q) + (1 - y_) * np.log(1 - q))
ml = min((optimize.minimize(nll_ad, [a0, 0.9, s0], method="L-BFGS-B", bounds=[(0, 1), (0, 1), (0.01, 200)])
          for a0 in (0.3, 0.6) for s0 in (3, 10, 30)), key=lambda r_: r_.fun)
print(f"Variant, Bernoulli maximum-likelihood fit on {len(sw_all)} trials: A = {ml.x[0]:.3f}, B = {ml.x[1]:.3f}, tau = {ml.x[2]:.2f} trials")
print("Trials per trial number after the switch:", sw_all.groupby("t").size().agg(["min", "max"]).to_dict())

Plotted proportions range 0.167 to 1.0

Result: reproduced. Over 14 switches between biased blocks, the proportion of choices toward the new block side is 0.543 in trials 0 to 4 and 0.827 in trials 20 to 39 (one-sided Fisher p = 2.7e-06). The fit gives A = 0.480, B = 1.000 (at its upper bound) and tau = 25.12 trials with a standard error of 16.14, so the time constant is poorly determined in one session. Resampling the switches (500 draws) gives 95% intervals of 0.279 to 0.643 for A, 0.836 to 1.000 for B and 6.41 to 38.37 trials for tau; B exceeds A in every draw, B is at its bound in 0.632 of them and tau is 40 trials or more in 0.018. A maximum-likelihood fit on the single trials, which weights each trial number by its count (10 to 14 trials), gives A = 0.479, B = 1.000 and tau = 25.03. At contrasts of 12.5% or less the pattern is the same (0.452 against 0.820; tau 21.57).

fig3b-contralateral-visual¶

Visual cortex (VISp) responds robustly to contralateral visual stimuli.

The files carry no atlas registration, so the test is in image coordinates (see the claims file).

mean_img = svd["mean_image"]
H, W = mean_img.shape
cols = np.arange(int(W * 0.3), int(W * 0.7))
midline = int(cols[np.argmin(mean_img[:, cols].mean(0))])
print(f"Midline estimate: column {midline} of {W} (lowest mean fluorescence in columns {cols[0]} to {cols[-1]})")
ev = wf.evoked(svt, onset)                       # trials x components
uim = svd["u"].reshape(len(svd["u"]), -1).astype(np.float64)

def peak_test(sel_trials):
    rmap = (ev[sel_trials & strong & right].mean(0) - ev[sel_trials & strong & ~right].mean(0)) @ uim
    res = {}
    for name, m in (("right_minus_left", rmap), ("left_minus_right", -rmap)):
        p = int(np.argmax(m)); y, x = divmod(p, W)
        res[name] = {"row": y, "col": x, "side": "left of midline" if x < midline else "right of midline", "value": m[p], "pixel": p}
    return rmap, res

all_trials = np.ones(len(trials), bool)
rmap, peaks = peak_test(all_trials)
for name, r in peaks.items():
    vals = ev @ uim[:, r["pixel"]]
    a, b = (vals[strong & right], vals[strong & ~right]) if name == "right_minus_left" else (vals[strong & ~right], vals[strong & right])
    _, p = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="greater")
    print(f"{name}: peak at row {r['row']}, column {r['col']} ({r['side']}), difference {r['value']:.4f} dF/F; "
          f"defining side {np.median(a):.4f} against other side {np.median(b):.4f} (median dF/F), one-sided Mann-Whitney p = {p:.2g}")
print("Peaks on opposite sides of the midline:", peaks["right_minus_left"]["side"] != peaks["left_minus_right"]["side"])
print(f"Mean image at the two peaks: {mean_img.ravel()[peaks['right_minus_left']['pixel']]:.0f} and "
      f"{mean_img.ravel()[peaks['left_minus_right']['pixel']]:.0f}; median over the frame {np.median(mean_img):.0f}, 5th percentile {np.percentile(mean_img, 5):.0f}")
for side, sel in (("right", strong & right), ("left", strong & ~right)):
    m = ev[sel].mean(0) @ uim
    p = int(np.argmax(m)); y, x = divmod(p, W)
    print(f"Peak of the {side}-stimulus evoked map itself: row {y}, column {x}, {m[p]:.4f} dF/F")

    _, p = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="greater")

# Time courses at the two all-trial masked peaks: defining-side stimulus minus other-side stimulus, baseline -0.3 to 0 s before
# the stimulus, aligned to the stimulus and to the movement onset, on trials at 25 or 100% with a movement onset after the stimulus.
moved = strong & (trials.rt > 0).to_numpy()
mo = wf.frame_index(frame_t, trials.wheel_movement_onset_time.fillna(trials.gabor_stimulus_onset_time).to_numpy())
tc_lags = np.arange(-10, 14)
rows_tc = {}
for name, p in masked_peaks.items():
    base = np.array([svt[o - 9:o].mean(0) for o in onset]) @ uim[:, p]
    for align, ev_frames in (("stimulus", onset), ("movement", mo)):
        tr_ = np.stack([svt[o + tc_lags] @ uim[:, p] for o in ev_frames]) - base[:, None]
        hi_side, lo_side = (moved & right, moved & ~right) if name == "right_minus_left" else (moved & ~right, moved & right)
        diff = tr_[hi_side].mean(0) - tr_[lo_side].mean(0)
        se = np.sqrt(tr_[hi_side].var(0, ddof=1) / hi_side.sum() + tr_[lo_side].var(0, ddof=1) / lo_side.sum())
        rows_tc[(f"{name} col {p % W}", f"{align}: diff")] = diff
        rows_tc[(f"{name} col {p % W}", f"{align}: z")] = diff / se
tc = pd.DataFrame(rows_tc, index=np.round(tc_lags / fps, 3))
tc.index.name = "s from event"
print(f"Trials: {int((moved & right).sum())} right, {int((moved & ~right).sum())} left stimulus; median movement onset {trials.rt[moved].median():.3f} s after the stimulus")
print(tc.round(4).to_string())

                    slow          13/14                         0.0982                        0.1020           0.5556            0.9806

Result: not reproduced. Under the criterion fixed beforehand, the peaks of the right-minus-left and left-minus-right maps both fall at the left edge of the frame (columns 0 and 2, rows 0 and 539), on the same side of the midline (column 316), with trial tests at p = 0.053 and 0.14. These corner pixels are darker in the mean image (534 and 926) than 95% of the frame (5th percentile 1538), so they lie outside the imaged brain; the spatial components cover the whole frame with no mask. In a variant restricted to pixels brighter than the median of the mean image and 20 pixels from the edge, the right-minus-left peak lies left of the midline (column 199) and the left-minus-right peak right of it (column 481), with p = 8.1e-15 and 1.6e-17.

The variants do not show that this lateralization is visual. On the trials at 25 or 100% contrast with a movement onset after the stimulus (162 right, 132 left), the side difference at the two masked peaks exceeds 3 standard errors from 0.128 s after the stimulus (z 3.3 and 3.7), while the median movement onset is 0.086 s. Aligned to the movement onset, the difference at the column 199 peak is already above zero 0.32 s before the onset (z 2.8), and at the column 481 peak from 0.03 s before it (z 2.4). Only 27 trials (13 right, 14 left) have no movement before 0.4 s. On them the difference at the two masked peaks points the same way (p = 0.02 and 0.091), but a masked peak search on these trials alone puts the right-minus-left peak right of the midline (column 550) and the left-minus-right peak left of it (column 72), the reverse of the search on all trials (p = 0.0062 and 0.012). This reversal is not explained here.

The slow trials exclude only wheel movement. Over the same 0.1 to 0.4 s window, paw speed and camera motion energy rise on most trials at 25 or 100% contrast, and several of them differ between right and left stimulus trials: wheel velocity, the right paw in both side cameras and the left camera's motion energy (p = 0.0005 or less). On the 27 slow trials, paw speed rises on 0.44 to 0.78 of trials and motion energy on 0.48 to 0.56, and the right paw in the right camera still differs by side (p = 0.014). So paw and face movements are not excluded on the slow trials, and over all trials they differ with the stimulus side in this window. Without an atlas registration neither the hemisphere nor VISp can be named. The variants do not change the outcome.

Encoding model¶

The design follows the claims file and wfprior.py. The body camera's video and motion-energy components are computed here by streaming the video from the archive.

Result: partially reproduced. The full model's cvR2 is 0.471 pooled in pixel space, 0.422 as the mean over pixels and 0.126 as the mean over components; with the intercept-only model (the time-point columns alone) subtracted, 0.123, 0.133 and 0.078. None is within 0.486 to 0.660; reading (a) is above 0.3, which the criterion counts as partial. No penalty is at either end of the grid for the full model. Four variants do not change the outcome. Over the masked pixels of the fig3b variant, reading (b) is 0.434. With folds that keep each trial's frames together and each frame once per trial, the full model's cvR2 falls to 0.422, 0.363 and 0.047, and to 0.068, 0.074 and 0.003 above the intercept-only model, so much of its gain over the intercept under the chiCa folds, which share frames of a trial between training and test rows, does not carry over to new trials. With the video components of the left and right cameras added, as in the paper, the notebook encoding_all_cameras.ipynb gives a full cvR2 of 0.574 (a) and 0.525 (b), within the range, and 0.208 (c); with folds by trial it is 0.472, 0.405 and 0.046, below the range again. The claims file fixed the body-camera design, so this does not decide the outcome. Without the body camera's components the pooled cvR2 falls from 0.471 to 0.414.

The paper is ambiguous on the reading. Its Results say the model accounts "for more than half of the total observed single trial variance" and give 0.60 and 0.54 as the full model's cvR2, while the Figure 4C legend says the full model is shown "with trial time regressor subtracted out". Under the subtracted reading the values here are 0.123 and 0.133 with the body camera and 0.226 and 0.236 with all three cameras (readings a and b), far below the range. The criterion's reading, without the subtraction, decides the outcome.

Result: partially reproduced. Shuffling the movement predictors lowers cvR2 by 0.104 (pooled), 0.119 (mean over pixels) and 0.067 (mean over components); shuffling the task predictors lowers it by 0.017, 0.015 and 0.013. Movement dominates under every reading and in every fold (smallest movement drop 0.065, largest task drop 0.019), but the movement drop is below the range 0.297 to 0.440 under every reading. The body camera's video components carry most of it: without them the movement drop is 0.042 pooled against 0.021 for task, and 0.010 against 0.015 over components. With folds by trial and each frame once per trial, the movement drop is 0.049, 0.060 and -0.005 against 0.017, 0.016 and 0.012 for task, so over components task exceeds movement, which under the criterion would count as not reproduced; the criterion's design uses the chiCa folds, so the outcome stays. With all three cameras (encoding_all_cameras.ipynb) the movement drop is 0.216, 0.232 and 0.161, still below the range, against 0.008, 0.008 and 0.007 for task; with folds by trial, 0.109, 0.115 and 0.008 against 0.008, 0.008 and 0.000.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. One session of one mouse, where the paper uses 10 sessions from each of 19 mice; the genotype is unknown, so values reported per genotype are compared with a range spanning both groups. The encoding model has no video components from the left and right cameras (left out for runtime; the notebook encoding_all_cameras.ipynb adds them as a variant), uses Lightning Pose paw speeds where the paper uses DeepLabCut, takes the ROI motion energies to be the whisker pads and body, and uses an action-kernel prior fitted here. The trial windows, the ridge penalty selection (generalized cross-validation) and the three readings of cvR2 are choices made here, as the paper's widefield code is not public; the lab's chiCa code sets the rest, including folds that split the frames of a trial between training and test rows. Reaction time is the trial table's wheel movement onset, which falls within 0.08 s of the stimulus or before it on more than half of the trials. VISp cannot be located without an atlas registration, so the visual response is tested in image coordinates.

What was found about the dandiset. It holds one session of one of the paper's 19 mice, and no genotype for its mouse. It has no published version. The atlas landmarks and registration that the conversion documentation describes are not in either file. The imaging planes give GCaMP6f where the paper and the file's keywords give GCaMP6s, the raw file states an imaging rate of 15 Hz where the timestamps give 31.2 Hz per channel, the dandiset's keywords name "CNTNALP2" where the paper and files name Nrxn1a, and the wheel's stated sign convention (counter-clockwise positive) is the opposite of what the choice labels imply. The trial table, wheel, licks and imaging are consistent with a shared clock.
